title: Judges 21:1–12
context: After the war, Israel grieves that one tribe is now missing, and the rash oath sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters to Benjamin traps them. Their solution is to destroy Jabesh Gilead, which had not come to the assembly, and to take its four hundred young women for the surviving Benjamites. The narrator reports these actions without approval, and the story shows how vows made in anger and solutions devised without seeking God compound evil with more evil. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly agree that the violence against Jabesh Gilead and the taking of its women are presented as part of Israel’s moral collapse, not as a model. The passage raises no doctrinal division between them.

verses.text: Now the men of Israel had sworn in Mizpah, saying, “None of us will give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the oath sworn at Mizpah not to give daughters to Benjamin. An oath made in anger now creates a crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rashness of the vow as a recurring theme in Judges (compare Judges 11:30). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against hasty vows (Ecclesiastes 5:2).

verses.text: The people came to Bethel and sat there until evening before God, and lifted up their voices, and wept severely.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people weeping before God at Bethel. Their grief over what has happened to a whole tribe of their own people is genuine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lament as recognizing the tragedy, though they will still seek solutions without fully seeking God’s counsel. Readers in both traditions commonly see sorrow without full repentance in these chapters.

verses.text: They said, “The LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that there should be one tribe lacking in Israel today?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the people’s question, asking why one tribe is now lacking in Israel. They bring their grief and confusion honestly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the question is addressed to God, though the loss resulted from Israel’s own actions. Both traditions commonly see the verse as an honest lament that does not yet acknowledge their own part.

verses.text: On the next day, the people rose early and built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people building an altar and offering burnt offerings and peace offerings. They seek God in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see worship here mixed with the confusion of the moment. Readers in both traditions commonly note that the text records no answer from God at this point.

verses.text: The children of Israel said, “Who is there among all the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up in the assembly to the LORD?” For they had made a great oath concerning him who didn’t come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, “He shall surely be put to death.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the second oath, that anyone who did not come to Mizpah would be put to death. Rash vows compound one another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how the second oath becomes the pretext for violence against Jabesh Gilead. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how oaths sworn in zeal can lead to further harm.

verses.text: The children of Israel grieved for Benjamin their brother, and said, “There is one tribe cut off from Israel today.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel grieving for Benjamin their brother and lamenting that a tribe is cut off. The sense of family loss is real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the grief as a recognition that Israel is one covenant people. Readers in both traditions commonly see the lament as appropriate, though the remedy they choose is not.

verses.text: How shall we provide wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them of our daughters to wives?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Israel’s dilemma: how to provide wives for the survivors while keeping their oath. They feel trapped by their own words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the dilemma as a consequence of a rash vow sworn in anger. Both traditions commonly read the verse as illustrating why Scripture warns against careless oaths (compare Matthew 5:37).

verses.text: They said, “What one is there of the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up to the LORD to Mizpah?” Behold, no one came from Jabesh Gilead to the camp to the assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people searching for any group that did not come to Mizpah, discovering that no one came from Jabesh Gilead. A solution is sought in legal technicality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inquiry as looking for a loophole rather than seeking God. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Jabesh Gilead later appears in Saul’s story (1 Samuel 11:1; 31:11).

verses.text: For when the people were counted, behold, there were none of the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead there.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the census confirms Jabesh Gilead’s absence. The people now feel justified in acting against them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confirmation as a step toward violence justified by the earlier oath. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a chain of decisions that the narrator presents critically.

verses.text: The congregation sent twelve thousand of the most valiant men there, and commanded them, saying, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead with the edge of the sword, with the women and the little ones.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the command to strike Jabesh Gilead, including women and children, as a grievous act of violence against fellow Israelites. The narrator reports it without approval.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the order as part of Israel’s moral collapse in this period. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sorrow, recognizing that zeal for an oath has overtaken justice and mercy.

verses.text: This is the thing that you shall do: you shall utterly destroy every male, and every woman who has lain with a man.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the instruction to destroy all except young women as deeply troubling, treating women as means to an end. The text does not hide the horror.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command as reflecting a distorted application of practices of destruction. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of what the book’s closing refrain judges, not as a model for God’s people.

verses.text: They found among the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead four hundred young virgins who had not known man by lying with him; and they brought them to the camp to Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the four hundred young women brought to the camp at Shiloh. Their lives have been taken from them by violence they did not choose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the women as victims of Israel’s attempt to solve one wrong with another. Readers in both traditions commonly honor their suffering and read the verse as part of the book’s portrait of collapse.
